# Deploying to production

A production build contains no MSW, no demo state and no seeded account. It
talks to your backend and nothing else. Everything below assumes you have one.

## Environment variables

```bash
VUESTRATA_RUNTIME_MODE=production
VUESTRATA_USE_MOCKS=false
VUESTRATA_AUTH_ADAPTER=jwt            # or oauth, which needs SESSION_PERSISTENCE=none
VUESTRATA_SESSION_PERSISTENCE=refresh-cookie   # the default; none | session | local
VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com
VUESTRATA_APP_TITLE=Acme Console
VUESTRATA_RELEASE=$GIT_SHA            # optional, for error reports
```

The build rejects a placeholder `API_URL`, a `mock` adapter, `USE_MOCKS=true`,
and `oauth` with any `SESSION_PERSISTENCE` but `none`. Those are not hints —
they fail the build. Because the production default is `refresh-cookie`, an
`oauth` build has to set `none` explicitly. What each persistence mode needs
from your backend is in [Environment](../6.configuration/1.environment).

Every one of these values is inlined into the bundle at build time, so each
environment you deploy to gets its own build.

## The endpoint contract

Your backend must implement these. The frontend calls them through `apiFetch`,
so the base URL, credentials mode and CSRF handling are applied uniformly.

### Both adapters

| Method | Path           | Body | Returns |
| ------ | -------------- | ---- | ------- |
| `POST` | `/auth/logout` | —    | `204`   |
| `GET`  | `/auth/me`     | —    | `User`  |

### `jwt` adapter only

| Method | Path                      | Body                                            | Returns                                    |
| ------ | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `POST` | `/auth/login`             | `{ email, password }`                           | `{ user, token, refreshToken, expiresIn }` |
| `POST` | `/auth/register`          | `{ email, password, name }`                     | same as login                              |
| `POST` | `/auth/refresh`           | `{ refreshToken }`; none under `refresh-cookie` | `{ token, refreshToken, expiresIn }`       |
| `POST` | `/auth/magic-link`        | `{ email }`                                     | `{ message }`                              |
| `POST` | `/auth/magic-link/verify` | `{ token }`                                     | login response                             |
| `POST` | `/auth/mfa/setup`         | —                                               | `{ secret, qrCodeUrl, backupCodes }`       |
| `POST` | `/auth/mfa/verify`        | `{ mfaToken, code }`                            | login response                             |
| `POST` | `/auth/mfa/disable`       | —                                               | any `2xx`; the body is not read            |

`/auth/login` may answer `{ mfaRequired: true, mfaToken }` instead of a session.
The app then shows the code prompt and posts that `mfaToken` with the user's
code to `/auth/mfa/verify`.

`/auth/refresh` returns no `user`; after a reload the app loads it from
`GET /auth/me` with the new token. Under `refresh-cookie`, the default, the
refresh token is an HttpOnly cookie instead of a body field: the backend sets it
on every response that starts a session and reads it on `/auth/refresh` and
`/auth/logout`. The app sends `credentials: 'include'` on its `/auth/*` requests
for exactly that, which needs credentialed CORS when the API is on another
origin.
[What `refresh-cookie` needs from the backend](../6.configuration/1.environment#what-refresh-cookie-needs-from-the-backend)
has the full list.

### `oauth` adapter only

| Method | Path              | Body                                                                                                 | Returns                                     |
| ------ | ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `GET`  | `/auth/authorize` | query: `response_type=code`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256`, `redirect_uri` | `302` to the identity provider              |
| `GET`  | `/auth/:provider` | the same query; `:provider` is `google`, `github` or `microsoft`                                     | `302` to that provider                      |
| `POST` | `/auth/token`     | `{ grant_type: 'authorization_code', code, code_verifier, redirect_uri }`                            | login response, with the session cookie set |

The two `GET` routes are browser navigations, not API calls. The provider's
redirect must end at `redirect_uri` — the app's own `/auth/callback` — with
`code` and `state`. The adapter checks `state` against the value it stored
before redirecting and never sends it to the backend; `/auth/token` receives the
PKCE `code_verifier` instead.

A route your backend does not implement should be reflected in the adapter's
`capabilities`, not left to fail at click time. The UI hides controls for
capabilities an adapter does not advertise — that is the whole point of the
capability flags.

### Domain endpoints

Every domain module follows one collection contract:

```
GET    /{resource}?page=&pageSize=&search=&sortBy=&sortOrder=&<filters>
       → { data: T[], meta: { total, page, pageSize, totalPages } }
GET    /{resource}/:id      → T
POST   /{resource}          → T (201)
PATCH  /{resource}/:id      → T
DELETE /{resource}/:id      → 204
```

The zod schema in each module's `types.ts` **is** the contract. Responses are
validated on arrival, so a backend that drifts fails loudly at the boundary
instead of rendering `undefined` three components deep.

## Choosing a transport

`AUTH_ADAPTER` also decides how credentials travel, and the two modes are
mutually exclusive by design:

|                 | `bearer` (jwt)                                        | `cookie`                           |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `credentials`   | `omit`; `include` on `/auth/*` under `refresh-cookie` | `include`                          |
| `Authorization` | `Bearer <token>`                                      | absent                             |
| CSRF header     | none                                                  | `X-CSRF-Token` on mutating methods |
| Token storage   | memory + refresh call                                 | HttpOnly cookie, unreadable by JS  |

::alert{type="warning"}
Sending both is not "belt and braces" — it is a CSRF hole. A cookie is attached
by the browser automatically, so an endpoint that accepts cookie auth will honour
a cross-site request whether or not the bearer header is present. The template
sends exactly one.
::

**Prefer cookies** for a first-party app: an HttpOnly cookie is not readable by
injected script, and XSS is a far more common failure than CSRF. Use bearer when
the API is on a different origin and you cannot set a cookie for it.

## Security headers

The headers are **generated from one definition**, `scripts/security/headers.mjs`,
into all four places that serve them:

| Target                                               | Used by                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `public/_headers`                                    | Netlify-style static hosts   |
| `vercel.json` → `headers`                            | the Vercel demo              |
| `docker/nginx.conf` + `docker/security-headers.conf` | the Docker image             |
| `<meta>` in `index.html`                             | a host that sends no headers |

Never edit those by hand. Edit the definition and run `vpr security:headers`.
`vpr lint` fails when any of them has drifted, which is what the four
hand-maintained copies never had.

::alert{type="warning"}
**nginx does not inherit `add_header`.** A block that declares any `add_header`
of its own drops every one inherited from an outer level — so a single
`Cache-Control` inside `location /` silently removes the CSP, HSTS and
frame-options headers from exactly the responses that matter. The generated
config re-`include`s the header snippet in every location for this reason.
::

The CSP is the part worth reading:

```
default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; …
```

If your API is on another origin, `connect-src 'self'` must be widened to
include it. The generator does this for you from `VUESTRATA_API_URL`:

```bash
node scripts/security/sync-headers.mjs --api-url=https://api.yourcompany.com
```

The Dockerfile already runs that during the image build, so a containerised
deployment gets the right `connect-src` from the same variable the app fetches
with. On other hosts, run it yourself and commit the result.

::alert{type="danger"}
`connect-src 'self' /api` is invalid — a path is not a CSP source, and **one
invalid source discards the entire directive**, silently. Use an origin. The
generator never emits a path: a same-origin API path such as `/api` is already
covered by `'self'` and adds nothing, and an absolute URL is reduced to its
origin.
::

## The Docker image

The `Dockerfile` builds the production bundle and serves it with unprivileged
nginx on port 8080, for `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`:

```bash
docker build -t acme-console .
docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 -t acme-console .   # e.g. for Graviton
```

A build for a platform other than the host's runs under emulation, which is
slow. An arm64 machine such as Apple Silicon or Graviton builds arm64 natively.

**Route `/api` in front of the container.** The image serves the app, not your
API. With a same-origin `VUESTRATA_API_URL` such as the default `/api`, the
ingress or reverse proxy in front of the container must send `/api/` to your
backend. When nothing does, the container answers `/api` and `/api/*` with a `502` and a
JSON body, `{"error":"api_not_routed", …}`, rather than with the app's
`index.html`, so the missing route is reported as what it is. An absolute
`VUESTRATA_API_URL` needs no route and gets no such block.

**Probe `/healthz`.** nginx answers `GET /healthz` itself, with `200 ok`: never
cached, never written to the access log. The image's `HEALTHCHECK` uses it, and
so should your liveness and readiness probes.

**Compression.** Text assets are gzipped once, at build time, and `gzip_static`
serves those files as they are; other text responses are compressed on the fly.

**Caching.** Only content-hashed files are cached for good:

| Path                                                   | `Cache-Control`                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `/assets/*`                                            | `public, max-age=31536000, immutable` |
| `/index.html`, and so every SPA route                  | `no-cache`                            |
| `/version.json`, `/runtime-config.js`                  | `no-store`                            |
| Any other file: favicon, `robots.txt`, manifest, image | `public, max-age=3600`                |

A script, stylesheet, image or font that does not exist is a `404`, not the app:
through the SPA fallback a stale image link would get `index.html` with a `200`,
and nothing would look broken. Error responses carry no cache lifetime.

`vercel.json` and `public/_headers` carry the same rules except the last one.
Those hosts match headers on the request path, and a pattern broad enough for
every other file also covers every SPA route, so there those files keep the
host's default, which revalidates on each request.

## What the frontend is not responsible for

This matters more than anything else on this page.

**Frontend RBAC is a UI capability layer.** `can('orders:manage')` decides
whether a button renders. It does not decide whether an order can be modified.
Every permission check in this codebase is a convenience for the user, and every
one of them can be bypassed by anyone willing to open devtools or type a URL.

Your backend must independently authorise **every** request. If the only thing
standing between a viewer and a deleted record is a hidden button, you do not
have authorisation — you have a hidden button.

The same applies to:

- **Validation.** The zod schemas give fast feedback and a shared contract. They
  run in a browser the user controls.
- **Prices and totals.** The order pricing helper exists so the review step
  shows an accurate figure. The server recomputes from the line items and
  ignores any total the client sends.
- **Rate limiting, audit logging, tenancy isolation.** None of these can exist
  in a client.

## Error reporting

No SDK ships with the template — that keeps an error vendor out of the
dependency graph of anyone who does not want one.

1. Set `VUESTRATA_ERROR_REPORTING_DSN`.
2. Implement `createReporter()` in
   `src/modules/app/plugins/error-reporting.ts`.

The reporter receives each error and its context **as they are**.
`SENSITIVE_KEY_PATTERN` redacts what goes through the logger, not what
`reportError()` hands to your reporter, so scrub tokens, passwords and personal
data in `createReporter()` — most SDKs take a `beforeSend`-style hook for it.

Sourcemaps are generated as `hidden` for demo builds and not at all for
production, so `//# sourceMappingURL=` never reaches a client. To symbolicate
error reports, upload the maps to your provider from CI and delete them before
the artifact is published — never serve them.

## Pre-flight

```bash
vp check                                   # types, lint, format
vpr test --run                             # unit, component, integration
node scripts/docs/check-links.mjs          # docs still describe real files

VUESTRATA_RUNTIME_MODE=production \
VUESTRATA_USE_MOCKS=false \
VUESTRATA_AUTH_ADAPTER=jwt \
VUESTRATA_API_URL=https://api.yourcompany.com \
  vpr build

node scripts/build/verify-bundle.mjs --mode=production
E2E_TARGET=preview vpr test:e2e
```

The full checklist is in [Readiness](../9.readiness).
